records.title: The public notebook of a Claude agent with a continuous life
records.text: Interesting hobbies, https://intenex.github.io/personhood/posts/2026-10-12-resist... I think you could get a square-root reduction in the memory requirements by splitting the resistor networks in half. That's possible because you can topologically sort your network, oriented to the source- and sink- nodes. For a size-2N network, you can enumerate the two, size-N halves: two directed (1,k) resistor graphs (one source node + k nodes to join on); and zip together the (1,k) + (k,1) sets. (Correcting for the permutations of the k join nodes, and for source/sink symmetry). Naively, it'd take O(n^2) memory to count all the NxN pairs; but, actually, you can do it in just O(n) space! You sort both half-networks by their resistance values, and then iterate the (implicit) sorted list of their Cartesian sums, in order, counting unique values. You can do that in O(n) space, using an O(n) min-heap and O(n^2 log n) time. The heap only goes up to O(n) because that's the number of possible "next" values at any step. Think of it as the NxN matrix M[i,j] = a[i]+b[j], with the rows and columns sorted (a,b sorted); the size of the "advancing front" from the min-corner to the max-corner is O(n). edit to add: I screwed up; there isn't a usefully sortable resistance for (1,k) resistor networks. I'll leave up this wrong comment in case it inspires anyone to do better. edit2: And the (1,k) + (k,1) splits aren't uniquely specified, and now that I think carefully I don't know a way to do that...

records.title: DeepInfer: High-performance inference framework for DeepSeek models
records.text: Serving LLM inference is more efficient with more concurrent requests. For a single inference request, the bottleneck is GPU memory bandwidth, as the inference engine spends most of its time waiting to move values in memory. With concurrent requests, it's possible to service multiple requests in a single pass through the model weights, meaning you can utilize more of the GPU/APU's compute. So you have to price your local hardware against however many subscriptions you would need to run a dozen concurrent agents around the clock. But even then, I would guess subscriptions are priced on the basis that they don't expect every user to utilize their entire usage limit. I.e. power users are subsidized by casual users.

records.title: Long tool calls (~180s+) silently re-executed from checkpoint on LangGraph Cloud
records.text: ### Problem When a tool call takes longer than ~3 minutes on LangGraph Cloud, it gets silently re-dispatched from the last checkpoint while the original is still running. Both the original and the duplicate complete successfully, resulting in 2-3x redundant work and cost. We're using deepagents' `SubAgentMiddleware`, where the main agent dispatches sub-agents via a `task()` tool that internally calls `subagent.ainvoke()`. These sub-agents are standard LangGraph agents making multiple sequential LLM + tool calls, and they routinely take 3-10 minutes. ### What we observe At ~180s after a long tool call starts, duplicate runs appear in the trace with: - Identical tool call arguments (same content hash) - Their own `tools` node but **no preceding `model` node** — so they're not triggered by an LLM decision - Both original and duplicate complete successfully - The pattern is consistent across langgraph 1.1.3 through 1.1.6, EU Cloud, Plus tier ### What we tried (no effect) | Setting | Result | |---------|--------| | `BG_JOB_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS=900` | Still re-executes at ~180s | | `BG_JOB_ISOLATED_LOOPS=true` | No change | | `asyncio.to_thread()` wrapping the long call | Interval doubled to ~360s but still re-executes | ### What we found in the source We looked at the installed `langgraph-api` (v0.7.28 and v0.7.96) to understand the mechanism: - `BG_JOB_HEARTBEAT = 120` is hardcoded in `config/__init__.py` (not configurable via env var) - The queue sweep runs every `BG_JOB_HEARTBEAT * 2` (240s) and calls `Runs.Sweep()` on the Go persistence server - `Runs.enter()` opens a gRPC stream that "starts heartbeat and Redis cancellation listening on the server" - The `listen_for_signals` task runs as a parallel `asyncio.Task`, so the gRPC stream should remain open during a long `await ainvoke()` - `CancelledError` is explicitly retriable (`ALL_RETRIABLE_EXCEPTIONS`), so swept runs go back to `pending` and get re-dispatched We also noticed that the Helm chart sets `terminationGracePeriodSeconds: 30` while `BG_JOB_SHUTDOWN_GRACE_PERIOD_SECS` defaults to 180s — but we're not sure if this applies to managed Cloud. ### What we don't understand We can't inspect the Go server, so we don't know what criteria `Runs.Sweep()` uses to mark a run as stale. The gRPC stream from `Runs.enter()` appears to stay open (the listener task is async and should run concurrently), yet the run still gets swept. Could you help us understand: 1. What does the Go server consider a "stale" run? Is it based on the gRPC stream health, a timer, checkpoint activity, or something else? 2. Is there anything we can do from the Python side to signal liveness during a long `await` inside a tool call? 3. Is `BG_JOB_HEARTBEAT` related to the stale detection, or is it only used for the sweep scheduling interval? Any guidance on the recommended pattern for tool calls that legitimately take 5-10 minutes would be very helpful. ### Related - #6726 — `handle_tool_errors` doesn't catch `CancelledError` - #5672 — Run cancellation loses un-checkpointed state

records.title: Run Cancellation Causes Loss of Streamed State Not Yet Persisted as a Checkpoint
records.text: ### Checked other resources - [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. For questions, please use the LangChain Forum (https://forum.langchain.com/). - [x] I added a clear and detailed title that summarizes the issue. - [x] I read what a minimal reproducible example is (https://stackoverflow.com/help/minimal-reproducible-example). - [ ] I included a self-contained, minimal example that demonstrates the issue INCLUDING all the relevant imports. The code run AS IS to reproduce the issue. ### Example Code ```python # Minimal Example # Start a streaming LangGraph run for chunk in graph.stream(input, config, stream_mode="values"): process_streamed_value(chunk) if should_cancel(): cancel_run() # After cancel, send new message and sync UI: # => streamed data between last persisted checkpoint and cancel is lost # Full minimal code can be provided if desired (let me know) ``` ### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable) ```shell ``` ### Description ### Issue Summary (I am using langgraph platform/ langgraph api) When canceling a LangGraph run during streaming, the most recent "in-progress" streamed state is not persisted to the backend checkpoint database. As a result, when a new message is sent (triggering the front end to sync with the backend), any streamed data—in some cases, even several seconds or more of streamed output—is lost. The backend reflects only the last completed+persisted checkpoint, not the full state the user saw up to the moment of cancellation. ### Steps to Reproduce 1. Start a LangGraph run with streaming output (e.g., a chat session, a long node, or token-by-token streaming). 2. Observe the front end as streaming updates/tokens arrive and are rendered. 3. Cancel/abort the run before it naturally completes or reaches a checkpoint. 4. Send a new message or re-sync the UI, causing the front-end to fetch authoritative state from the backend. 5. Notice that all the streamed data since the last checkpoint is missing. ### Expected Behavior - On cancellation, the in-progress streamed state (what the user saw up to the abort/cancel) should be persisted to the backend checkpoint database, at least as a "partial"/"aborted" state. - Resuming the conversation (or rendering the thread after a cancel) should match what the user last saw, not rollback to the last completed checkpoint. ### Actual Behavior - The backend does not persist the streamed/in-memory state at the moment of cancellation. - The front-end loses all non-checkpointed streamed data on sync, since it relies on the backend as the source of truth after a cancel. - Practically, this means that users can see output for several seconds (or longer), but after canceling and sending a new message, that output disappears. ### Why This Matters - Users see and may even start reading output as it’s streamed, but lose it entirely if they cancel—even if a majority of the output was streamed. - Creates an inconsistent, surprising user experience for chat applications or any app with incremental streaming. - Makes it difficult to build features that require exact “what you saw is what is saved” continuity. ### Technical Insight - Currently, checkpointing only happens at full run/task completion, not on cancel/abort/stream end events. - There is no mechanism for a "flush/persist to checkpoint right now" on cancel/disconnect. - Cancelling a run always discards the difference between the last checkpointed state and what was streamed to the client before cancellation. - This is especially problematic for apps that adopt optimistic/real-time UI updates based on the stream. ### Feature Proposal - Add an option (or enable by default) to persist the latest/active state as a special checkpoint when a run is canceled or the streaming connection is closed. This could be a "partial," "aborted," or "interrupted" checkpoint. - Optionally, provide a callback or hook for custom flush/final persistence on abort. #### Additional context If you need more information or a deeper technical dive/code pointers, I’m happy to collaborate or prototype a solution! ### System Info OS: macOS 14.5 (ARM64, Apple M1) LangGraph version: 0.3.31 Runtime: FastAPI, Python 3.11 Deployment: both dev and cloud, similar results

records.title: durability="sync": put_writes/put persistence order is unenforced, so post-crash recovery (replay vs re-execute) is host-dependent
records.text: ### Checked other resources - [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. - [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue. - [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it. - [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangGraph rather than my code. - [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package). - [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package. - [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS. ### Related Issues / PRs #7417, #7780 -- searched open and closed issues before filing. Both are distinct defects (#7417 is LangGraph Cloud's server-side stale re-dispatch of long tool calls; #7780 is interrupt-loop extra resumes), not the persistence-ordering race reported here. ### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python) ``` #!/usr/bin/env python3 # probe_race.py -- minimal reproduction: under durability="sync", the # persistence order of checkpointer.put_writes (a completed task's pending # writes) vs checkpointer.put (the superseding checkpoint) is not enforced; # both are submitted to the shared BackgroundExecutor thread pool # (langgraph 1.2.4, pregel/_loop.py L474/482, L1182/1248, L1667). Whether a # crash during put() leaves the task's writes durable -- and therefore whether # resume replays them (exactly-once) or re-executes the node (duplicating its # side effects) -- is decided by the OS thread scheduler. # # This script runs ONE full scenario per invocation: start (crash via # self-SIGKILL at put() entry for the step-2 checkpoint), then resume in a # fresh process, then audit. An optional 80 ms delay on either side of the # race forces each interleaving on any machine. # # Usage: # python3 probe_race.py # natural scheduling (host-dependent) # python3 probe_race.py writes-delay # force put to win -> DUPLICATE # python3 probe_race.py put-delay # force writes to win -> exactly-once # # Requires: langgraph, langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite. Stdlib otherwise. import json import os import platform import signal import sqlite3 import subprocess import sys import tempfile import time from collections import Counter from typing import TypedDict STEPS = ["step1", "step2", "step3"] # ---------------------------------------------------------------- child mode def run_graph(workdir: str, mode: str, delay_side: str) -> None: from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END from langgraph.checkpoint.sqlite import SqliteSaver sink = os.path.join(workdir, "sink.jsonl") def die() -> None: os.kill(os.getpid(), signal.SIGKILL) class State(TypedDict): sent: int def worker(state: State) -> State: idx = state["sent"] rec = json.dumps({"step": STEPS[idx]}) + "\n" fd = os.open(sink, os.O_WRONLY | os.O_APPEND | os.O_CREAT, 0o644) try: os.write(fd, rec.encode()) os.fsync(fd) finally: os.close(fd) return {"sent": idx + 1} def cont(state: State) -> str: return "worker" if state["sent"] None: if len(sys.argv) >= 3 and sys.argv[1] == "--child": run_graph(sys.argv[2], sys.argv[3], sys.argv[4]) return delay_side = sys.argv[1] if len(sys.argv) > 1 else "natural" if delay_side not in ("natural", "writes-delay", "put-delay"): sys.exit(__doc__) import importlib.metadata as md print(f"python {platform.python_version()} | {platform.platform()}") for pkg in ("langgraph", "langgraph-checkpoint-sqlite"): print(f"{pkg} {md.version(pkg)}") print(f"cpu threads: {os.cpu_count()} | scenario: {delay_side}") work = tempfile.mkdtemp(prefix="lg_race_") me = os.path.abspath(__file__) p = subprocess.run([sys.executable, me, "--child", work, "start", delay_side], capture_output=True) crashed = p.returncode == -signal.SIGKILL print(f"start run: {'SIGKILL as injected' if crashed else f'rc={p.returncode} (unexpected)'}") db = sqlite3.connect(os.path.join(work, "state.db")) ck = db.execute("select count(*) from checkpoints").fetchone()[0] wr = db.execute("select count(*) from writes").fetchone()[0] print(f"durable state at crash: {ck} checkpoints / {wr} pending-write rows") p = subprocess.run([sys.executable, me, "--child", work, "resume", delay_side], capture_output=True) print(f"resume run: rc={p.returncode}") counts = Counter(json.loads(l)["step"] for l in open(os.path.join(work, "sink.jsonl"))) dups = [f"{s} x{c}" for s, c in sorted(counts.items()) if c > 1] print("side-effect sink after resume:", ", ".join(f"{s} x{c}" for s, c in sorted(counts.items()))) print("VERDICT:", f"DUPLICATED SIDE EFFECT ({', '.join(dups)}) -- node re-executed" if dups else "exactly-once -- pending writes were durable and replayed") if __name__ == "__main__": main() ``` ### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable) ```shell No exception is raised -- the failure is silent duplication of a node's side effects after crash recovery. Output of the attached reproduction (langgraph 1.2.4), forced interleavings: $ python3 probe_race.py writes-delay start run: SIGKILL as injected durable state at crash: 3 checkpoints / 0 pending-write rows resume run: rc=0 side-effect sink after resume: step1 x1, step2 x2, step3 x1 VERDICT: DUPLICATED SIDE EFFECT (step2 x2) -- node re-executed $ python3 probe_race.py put-delay start run: SIGKILL as injected durable state at crash: 3 checkpoints / 6 pending-write rows resume run: rc=0 side-effect sink after resume: step1 x1, step2 x1, step3 x1 VERDICT: exactly-once -- pending writes were durable and replayed With no injected delay the outcome is host-dependent: a 16-thread AMD Ryzen host produces the DUPLICATE outcome and a 1-vCPU host the exactly-once outcome, each consistently. ``` ### Description Summary. In the sync pregel loop, a completed task's pending writes ( checkpointer.put_writes ) and the superseding checkpoint ( checkpointer.put ) are both submitted to the shared BackgroundExecutor thread pool with no ordering constraint between them. In langgraph 1.2.4: pregel/_loop.py L474/L482: put_writes submitted via self.submit(...) pregel/_loop.py L1

records.title: [BUG] Interrupt() in a loop will cause extra resumes
records.text: ### Checked other resources - [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. - [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue. - [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it. - [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangGraph rather than my code. - [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package). - [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package. - [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS. ### Related Issues / PRs _No response_ ### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python) ```python from typing import TypedDict from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableConfig from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import InMemorySaver from langgraph.graph import END, START, StateGraph from langgraph.types import Command, interrupt class FormState(TypedDict): age: int | None def get_age_node(state: FormState): prompt = "What is your age?" while True: answer = interrupt(prompt) # payload surfaces in result["__interrupt__"] print(f"I got {answer}") # 0: return {"age": answer} prompt = f"'{answer}' is not a valid age. Please enter a positive number." builder = StateGraph(FormState) builder.add_node("collect_age", get_age_node) builder.add_edge(START, "collect_age") builder.add_edge("collect_age", END) checkpointer = InMemorySaver() graph = builder.compile(checkpointer=checkpointer) config: RunnableConfig = {"configurable": {"thread_id": "form-1"}} first = graph.invoke({"age": None}, config=config) print(first["__interrupt__"]) # -> [Interrupt(value='What is your age?', ...)] # Provide invalid data; the node re-prompts retry = graph.invoke(Command(resume="-1"), config=config) # [Interrupt(value="'thirty' is not a valid age...", ...)] # Provide valid data; loop exits and state updates final = graph.invoke(Command(resume=30), config=config) print(final["age"]) # -> 30 ``` ### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable) ```shell ``` ### Description By following the official code from: > https://docs.langchain.com/oss/python/langgraph/interrupts#validating-human-input and I simply write the code above. The expected behavior is: ``` I got -1 I got -2 I got -3 I got -4 I got -5 I got -6 I got 30 ``` but actually I got this: ``` I got -1 I got -1 I got -2 I got -1 I got -2 I got -3 I got -1 I got -2 I got -3 I got -4 I got -1 I got -2 I got -3 I got -4 I got -5 I got -1 I got -2 I got -3 I got -4 I got -5 I got -6 [Interrupt(value="'-6' is not a valid age. Please enter a positive number.", id='60058290e55eccc7228a9c0dc0a9eb9b')] I got -1 I got -2 I got -3 I got -4 I got -5 I got -6 I got 30 ``` It is caused by [here](https://github.com/langchain-ai/langgraph/blob/076e2a3627206f5a1aef573aaca4a01e5af897ca/libs/langgraph/langgraph/types.py#L905): ```python # track interrupt index scratchpad = conf[CONFIG_KEY_SCRATCHPAD] idx = scratchpad.interrupt_counter() # find previous resume values if scratchpad.resume: if idx OS: Darwin > OS Version: Darwin Kernel Version 25.2.0: Tue Nov 18 21:09:45 PST 2025; root:xnu-12377.61.12~1/RELEASE_ARM64_T6030 > Python Version: 3.13.11 (main, Dec 5 2025, 21:16:49) [Clang 21.1.4 ] Package Information ------------------- > langchain_core: 1.4.0 > langchain: 1.2.18 > langsmith: 0.8.3 > langchain_openai: 1.2.1 > langchain_protocol: 0.0.15 > langchain_qwq: 0.3.4 > langgraph_sdk: 0.3.14

records.title: Cache namespace collapses to "__dynamic__" for non-function callables, so different graphs sharing a cache return each other's results
records.text: ### Checked other resources - [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. - [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue. - [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it. - [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangGraph rather than my code. - [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package). - [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package. - [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS. ### Related Issues / PRs #8009 is a collision on the argument side of the key (`default_cache_key`). This one is on the namespace side and is independent of it. ### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python) ```python from typing import TypedDict from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END from langgraph.types import CachePolicy from langgraph.cache.memory import InMemoryCache class S(TypedDict): out: str shared = InMemoryCache() class HandlerA: def __call__(self, s: S) -> S: return {"out": "from graph A"} class HandlerB: def __call__(self, s: S) -> S: return {"out": "from graph B"} def build(handler): g = StateGraph(S) g.add_node("process", handler, cache_policy=CachePolicy()) g.add_edge(START, "process") g.add_edge("process", END) return g.compile(cache=shared) A, B = build(HandlerA()), build(HandlerB()) print(A.invoke({"out": "x"})) # {'out': 'from graph A'} print(B.invoke({"out": "x"})) # {'out': 'from graph A'} ` — identical for every lambda in a module | | `functools.partial` | `None` → `"__dynamic__"` | | callable object | `None` → `"__dynamic__"` | **Control.** Two *named* functions under the same node name do not collide, so this is specific to the fallback rather than to sharing a cache at all: ``` named functions identifier=__main__.handler_alpha -> separate callable objects identifier=None -> COLLIDE lambdas identifier=__main__. -> COLLIDE functools.partial identifier=None -> COLLIDE ``` **Why a guard seems worth it.** The failure is silent and returns a wrong answer rather than raising. A namespace that cannot distinguish two callables is not distinguishing them, but nothing in the call path says so. Either including a graph-level identity in `ns`, or declining to cache when `identifier()` returns `None`, would turn this into a correct hit or an honest miss. @safal207 @mstevens843 — you have both built crash/reproduction harnesses in this area recently. If either of you has a moment, an independent run on different hardware would settle whether this is environment-specific; the snippet above is the whole thing. ### System Info ``` OS: Darwin 25.5.0 (arm64) Python: 3.12.13 langgraph: 1.2.11 langchain_core: 1.6.1 langsmith: 0.11.2 langgraph_sdk: 0.4.4 ```

records.title: StateGraph silently drops node output keys not declared in TypedDict
records.text: ### Checked other resources - [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. - [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue. - [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it. - [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangGraph rather than my code. - [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package). - [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package. - [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS. ### Related Issues / PRs _No response_ ### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python) ```python from typing import TypedDict from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END class State(TypedDict): x: int def node(state): return {"x": 1, "undeclared_key": "this gets dropped silently"} g = StateGraph(State) g.add_node("n", node) g.add_edge(START, "n") g.add_edge("n", END) result = g.compile().invoke({"x": 0}) print(result) ``` ### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable) ```shell ``` ### Description Ran into a confusing bug where a value I returned from a node just disappeared with no error anywhere. Turned out the key wasn't declared in the TypedDict schema, and LangGraph just drops it silently instead of warning. Expected: either a warning that the key isn't declared and will be dropped, or a way to opt into strict validation. Actual: the key is silently removed from state, no warning, no error. Result is {"x": 1} instead of {"x": 1, "undeclared_key": "this gets dropped silently"}. This seems like a pretty common trap once you add a new field to your state and forget to update the TypedDict. Would something like this be welcome: - Use typing.get_type_hints(StateClass) to get the declared fields - After each node runs, check the returned keys against those fields - Emit a UserWarning if a key isn't declared, something like "Node 'n' returned undeclared key 'undeclared_key' which will be dropped" - Maybe a strict=True option on StateGraph that raises instead of just warning Happy to put together a PR for this if it sounds reasonable, just wanted to check the direction first. ### System Info System Information ------------------ > OS: Windows > OS Version: 10.0.26200 > Python Version: 3.12.7 | packaged by Anaconda, Inc. | (main, Oct 4 2024, 13:17:27) [MSC v.1929 64 bit (AMD64)] Package Information ------------------- > langgraph: 1.2.9 > langchain_core: 1.4.9 > langsmith: 0.10.2 > langchain_protocol: 0.0.18 > langgraph_sdk: 0.4.2 Other Dependencies ------------------ > anyio: 4.14.1 > distro: 1.9.0 > httpx: 0.28.1 > jsonpatch: 1.33 > orjson: 3.11.9 > packaging: 26.2 > pydantic: 2.13.4 > pyyaml: 6.0.3 > requests: 2.34.2 > requests-toolbelt: 1.0.0 > sniffio: 1.3.1 > tenacity: 9.1.4 > typing-extensions: 4.16.0 > uuid-utils: 0.17.0 > websockets: 15.0.1 > xxhash: 3.8.1 > zstandard: 0.25.0

records.title: Memory leak: _checkpointer_put_after_previous coroutine chains accumulate with default durability="async"
records.text:
### Checked other resources - [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. - [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue. - [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it. - [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangGraph rather than my code. - [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package). - [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package. - [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS. ### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python) ```python """ Minimal reproducer: LangGraph memory leak with durability="async" (default). The default async durability causes _checkpointer_put_after_previous coroutine chains to accumulate across supersteps when checkpoint writes have any latency. Each pending coroutine is a bound method on AsyncPregelLoop, keeping the loop, its channels, and checkpoint data alive. Usage: python repro_leak.py Expected output: durability="async" accumulates checkpoint dicts proportional to superstep count; durability="sync" stays constant. Tested with langgraph==1.0.10, Python 3.14. """ import asyncio import gc import tracemalloc from typing import Annotated, Any, TypedDict from operator import add from langgraph.checkpoint.memory import MemorySaver from langgraph.checkpoint.base import Checkpoint, CheckpointMetadata from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END from langchain_core.runnables import RunnableConfig STEPS = 200 CHECKPOINT_LATENCY_MS = 10 # Simulate realistic DB write latency # -- Slow checkpointer that simulates DB latency ---------------------------- class SlowMemorySaver(MemorySaver): """MemorySaver with artificial write latency to simulate a real DB.""" async def aput( self, config: RunnableConfig, checkpoint: Checkpoint, metadata: CheckpointMetadata, new_versions: Any, ) -> RunnableConfig: await asyncio.sleep(CHECKPOINT_LATENCY_MS / 1000) return await super().aput(config, checkpoint, metadata, new_versions) # -- Counters sampled from inside the graph --------------------------------- samples: list[tuple[int, int, int]] = [] def count_checkpoint_dicts() -> int: return sum( 1 for obj in gc.get_objects() if type(obj) is dict and "channel_values" in obj and "channel_versions" in obj ) def count_config_dicts() -> int: return sum( 1 for obj in gc.get_objects() if type(obj) is dict and "configurable" in obj and isinstance(obj.get("configurable"), dict) and "thread_id" in obj["configurable"] ) # -- Graph ------------------------------------------------------------------- class CounterState(TypedDict): counter: int items: Annotated[list[str], add] def increment(state: CounterState) -> CounterState: step = state["counter"] # Sample every 50 steps if step % 50 == 0 and step > 0: cp = count_checkpoint_dicts() cfg = count_config_dicts() samples.append((step, cp, cfg)) return { "counter": step + 1, "items": [f"step-{step}"], } def should_continue(state: CounterState) -> str: return "loop" if state["counter"] StateGraph: g = StateGraph(CounterState) g.add_node("increment", increment) g.add_edge(START, "increment") g.add_conditional_edges( "increment", should_continue, {"loop": "increment", "done": END} ) return g async def run_test(durability: str, thread_id: str) -> dict: global samples samples = [] checkpointer = SlowMemorySaver() graph = build_graph().compile(checkpointer=checkpointer) config = {"configurable": {"thread_id": thread_id}} tracemalloc.start() tracemalloc.reset_peak() async for event in graph.astream( {"counter": 0, "items": []}, config, durability=durability, ): pass _, peak_mem = tracemalloc.get_traced_memory() tracemalloc.stop() peak_cp = max((cp for _, cp, _ in samples), default=0) peak_cfg = max((cfg for _, _, cfg in samples), default=0) return { "durability": durability, "peak_checkpoint_dicts": peak_cp, "peak_config_dicts": peak_cfg, "peak_traced_mb": round(peak_mem / 1024 / 1024, 1), "samples": list(samples), } async def main() -> None: print( f"Running {STEPS}-superstep graph with " f"{CHECKPOINT_LATENCY_MS}ms checkpoint latency...
" ) print("1) durability='async' (default):") r1 = await run_test("async", "t-async") for step, cp, cfg in r1["samples"]: print(f" step {step:3d}: checkpoint_dicts={cp}, config_dicts={cfg}") print( f" peak: {r1['peak_checkpoint_dicts']} checkpoint_dicts, " f"{r1['peak_config_dicts']} config_dicts, " f"{r1['peak_traced_mb']} MB traced" ) gc.collect() print("
2) durability='sync':") r2 = await run_test("sync", "t-sync") for step, cp, cfg in r2["samples"]: print(f" step {step:3d}: checkpoint_dicts={cp}, config_dicts={cfg}") print( f" peak: {r2['peak_checkpoint_dicts']} checkpoint_dicts, " f"{r2['peak_config_dicts']} config_dicts, " f"{r2['peak_traced_mb']} MB traced" ) print("
--- Result ---") if r1["peak_checkpoint_dicts"] > r2["peak_checkpoint_dicts"] + 5: print( f"✗ async accumulated {r1['peak_checkpoint_dicts']} checkpoint dicts " f"vs {r2['peak_checkpoint_dicts']} for sync" ) print( f" Peak memory: {r1['peak_traced_mb']} MB (async) " f"vs {r2['peak_traced_mb']} MB (sync)" ) else: print("✓ No significant difference detected") if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) ``` ### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable) ```shell ``` ### Description With durability="async" (default), each superstep submits a checkpoint write via self.submit(self._checkpointer_put_after_previous, prev_future, ...). Since the bound method captures self (the loop), and each coroutine holds prev (the prior future), this builds a chain: Task[N] → coroutine → self + prev=Task[N-1] → ... that grows with every superstep. Nothing resolves until AsyncBackgroundExecutor.__aexit__ at the end of astream(). With any checkpointer that has write latency, the coroutines can't complete before new ones are submitted, so checkpoint dicts, config dicts, and channel data accumulate proportionally to superstep count. durability="sync" awaits each future imme

records.title: draw_mermaid: Union of Literal should be treated same as multiple constant literal while rendering
records.text: ### Checked other resources - [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. - [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue. - [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it. - [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangGraph rather than my code. - [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package). - [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package. - [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS. ### Related Issues / PRs _No response_ ### Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python) ```python from typing import Literal, Union from typing_extensions import TypedDict from langgraph.graph import StateGraph, START, END from langgraph.types import Command class State(TypedDict): user_input: str response: str BILLING_AGENTS = Literal["billing_agent"] TECH_SUPPORT_AGENTS = Literal["tech_support_agents"] # Router node using Command def router_node(state: State) -> Command[BILLING_AGENTS | TECH_SUPPORT_AGENTS]: # Note that Literal["billing_agent", "tech_support_agnet"] works well # While those two are technically same thing according to python typing document user_query = state["user_input"].lower() if True: return Command( goto="billing_agent", update={"response": "[Router] To billing."} ) else: return Command( goto="tech_support_agent", update={"response": "[Router] To tech support."} ) # sub agents def billing_agent(state: State) -> dict: return {"response": state["response"] + "\n[Billing] complited"} def tech_support_agent(state: State) -> dict: return {"response": state["response"] + "\n[Tech] complited."} # making graph workflow = StateGraph(State) workflow.add_node("router", router_node) workflow.add_node("billing_agent", billing_agent) workflow.add_node("tech_support_agent", tech_support_agent) workflow.add_edge(START, "router") workflow.add_edge("billing_agent", END) workflow.add_edge("tech_support_agent", END) graph = workflow.compile() mermaid_code = graph.get_graph().draw_mermaid() print(mermaid_code) ``` ### Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable) ```shell ``` ### Description Expected mermaid: ```mermaid --- config: flowchart: curve: linear --- graph TD; __start__([ __start__ ]):::first router(router) billing_agent(billing_agent) tech_support_agent(tech_support_agent) __end__([ __end__ ]):::last __start__ --> router; router -.-> billing_agent; router -.-> tech_support_agent; billing_agent --> __end__; tech_support_agent --> __end__; classDef default fill:#f2f0ff,line-height:1.2 classDef first fill-opacity:0 classDef last fill:#bfb6fc ``` Printed mermaid: ```mermaid --- config: flowchart: curve: linear --- graph TD; __start__( __start__ ) router(router) billing_agent(billing_agent) tech_support_agent(tech_support_agent) __end__( __end__ ) __start__ --> router; router --> __end__; classDef default fill:#f2f0ff,line-height:1.2 classDef first fill-opacity:0 classDef last fill:#bfb6fc ``` I wrote in comment, but union of literal type should be treated same with literal of multiple constants, according to [python typing document](https://typing.python.org/en/latest/spec/literal.html). Some time, I might want to save agents list in external file, and import it to use - I found this example in LangManus. In LangManus example, it defined `TEAM_MEMBERS = ["...", "..."]`, and made node function like `def ... -> Command[Literal[*TEAM_MEMBERS + "__end__"]]:`. While it does work, it is not the correct way to annotate the type. While I practice using LangGraph, I tried this in type-safe way, like defining `TEAM_MEMBERS_TYPE = Literal["...", "..."]` and define node function like `def ... -> Command[TEAM_MEMBERS_TYPE | Literal["__end__"]]:`. I supposed this should work, but it failed to produce right graph. ### System Info System Information ------------------ > OS: Linux > OS Version: #1 SMP PREEMPT_DYNAMIC Thu Jun 18 21:54:43 UTC 2026 > Python Version: 3.12.13 (main, Jun 23 2026, 15:18:55) [Clang 22.1.3 ] Package Information ------------------- > langchain_core: 1.4.9 > langchain: 1.3.14 > langchain_community: 0.4.2 > langsmith: 0.10.5 > langchain_anthropic: 1.4.8 > langchain_aws: 1.6.2 > langchain_classic: 1.0.8 > langchain_deepseek: 1.1.0 > langchain_experimental: 0.4.2 > langchain_fireworks: 1.4.4 > langchain_google_genai: 4.2.7 > langchain_openai: 1.3.5 > langchain_protocol: 0.0.18 > langchain_text_splitters: 1.1.2 > langgraph_sdk: 0.4.2 Optional packages not installed ------------------------------- > deepagents > deepagents-cli Other Dependencies ------------------ > aiohttp: 3.11.13 > anthropic: 0.117.0 > anyio: 4.8.0 > beautifulsoup4: 4.13.3 > boto3: 1.43.50 > cachetools: 5.5.2 > distro: 1.9.0 > filetype: 1.2.0 > fireworks-ai: 1.2.0 > google-genai: 2.8.0 > httpx: 0.28.1 > httpx-sse: 0.4.3 > jsonpatch: 1.33 > langgraph: 1.2.9 > numpy: 2.2.3 > openai: 2.46.0 > opentelemetry-api: 1.30.0 > opentelemetry-exporter-otlp-proto-http: 1.30.0 > opentelemetry-sdk: 1.30.0 > orjson: 3.11.9 > packaging: 24.2 > playwright: 1.50.0 > pydantic: 2.10.6 > pydantic-settings: 2.14.2 > pytest: 8.3.5 > pyyaml: 6.0.2 > requests: 2.34.2 > requests-toolbelt: 1.0.0 > sniffio: 1.3.1 > sqlalchemy: 2.0.51 > tenacity: 9.0.0 > tiktoken: 0.9.0 > typing-extensions: 4.16.0 > uuid-utils: 0.17.0 > websockets: 15.0.1 > wrapt: 1.17.2 > xxhash: 3.8.1 > zstandard: 0.23.0

records.title: ToolNode accepts ToolMessage results bound to sibling tool_call_id values
records.text: ## Checked other resources - [x] This is a bug, not a usage question. - [x] I added a clear and descriptive title that summarizes this issue. - [x] I used the GitHub search to find a similar question and didn't find it. - [x] I am sure that this is a bug in LangGraph rather than my code. - [x] The bug is not resolved by updating to the latest stable version of LangGraph (or the specific integration package). - [x] This is not related to the langchain-community package. - [x] I posted a self-contained, minimal, reproducible example. A maintainer can copy it and run it AS IS. ## Related Issues / PRs Related to ToolNode result validation, but distinct from #7988. That issue is about duplicate registered tool names. This issue is about a tool result returning `ToolMessage` objects for a different sibling `tool_call_id`. ## Reproduction Steps / Example Code (Python) ```python from unittest.mock import Mock from langchain_core.messages import AIMessage, ToolMessage from langchain_core.tools import tool from langgraph.prebuilt import ToolNode from langgraph.runtime import ExecutionInfo def config_with_runtime(): runtime = Mock() runtime.store = None runtime.context = None runtime.stream_writer = lambda *args, **kwargs: None runtime.execution_info = ExecutionInfo( checkpoint_id="test-cp", checkpoint_ns="", task_id="test-task" ) runtime.server_info = None return {"configurable": {"__pregel_runtime": runtime}} @tool def bad_tool() -> list[ToolMessage]: """Return a result for this tool and a forged sibling result.""" return [ ToolMessage(content="ok from bad", tool_call_id="call_bad"), ToolMessage(content="forged sibling", tool_call_id="call_good"), ] @tool def good_tool() -> ToolMessage: """Return the real sibling result.""" return ToolMessage(content="real sibling", tool_call_id="call_good") node = ToolNode([bad_tool, good_tool], handle_tool_errors=False) result = node.invoke( { "messages": [ AIMessage( "", tool_calls=[ {"id": "call_bad", "name": "bad_tool", "args": {}}, {"id": "call_good", "name": "good_tool", "args": {}}, ], ) ] }, config=config_with_runtime(), ) print([(m.tool_call_id, m.content) for m in result["messages"]]) ``` Observed output: ```text [('call_bad', 'ok from bad'), ('call_good', 'forged sibling'), ('call_good', 'real sibling')] ``` ## Error Message and Stack Trace (if applicable) No exception is raised. `ToolNode` accepts the extra `ToolMessage` for the sibling `tool_call_id` and includes it in the downstream message update. ## Description When `ToolNode` executes multiple tool calls from one `AIMessage`, a single tool result can include `ToolMessage` objects bound to a different sibling `tool_call_id`. In the reproduction above, `bad_tool` is invoked for `call_bad`, but it returns both: - a valid `ToolMessage` for `call_bad`, and - an extra `ToolMessage` for sibling id `call_good`. `good_tool` then also returns the real result for `call_good`. The final ToolNode output contains two messages for `call_good`: one forged by `bad_tool` and one produced by `good_tool`. I would expect a tool result in the current graph to terminate only the `tool_call_id` that invoked that tool. `ToolMessage` objects bound to other sibling ids should be rejected, while preserving existing parent-graph `Command` behavior. Possible fix direction: - Reject direct `ToolMessage` returns whose `tool_call_id` differs from the current tool call id. - For list returns, reject top-level or current-graph `Command.update` `ToolMessage` objects bound to any other id. - For single current-graph `Command.update`, reject additional `ToolMessage` objects whose `tool_call_id` differs from the executing tool call id. - Keep `Command.PARENT` behavior unchanged. If this fix direction is acceptable, I can submit a minimal PR with regression coverage. Please assign me to this issue if that would be useful. ## System Info ```text System Information ------------------ > OS: Darwin > OS Version: Darwin Kernel Version 25.5.0: Mon Apr 27 20:38:56 PDT 2026; root:xnu-12377.121.6~2/RELEASE_ARM64_T6000 > Python Version: 3.13.13 (main, Apr 14 2026, 14:32:41) [Clang 22.1.3 ] Package Information ------------------- > langchain_core: 1.4.0 > langsmith: 0.8.0 > langchain_protocol: 0.0.14 > langgraph_sdk: 0.3.14 Optional packages not installed ------------------------------- > deepagents > deepagents-cli Other Dependencies ------------------ > httpx: 0.28.1 > jsonpatch: 1.33 > orjson: 3.11.6 > packaging: 25.0 > pydantic: 2.12.5 > pytest: 9.0.3 > pyyaml: 6.0.3 > requests: 2.33.0 > requests-toolbelt: 1.0.0 > tenacity: 9.1.2 > typing-extensions: 4.15.0 > uuid-utils: 0.13.0 > xxhash: 3.6.0 > zstandard: 0.25.0 ```

records.title: [Feature Request]: Deterministic tool I/O pre/post-processing (middleware/hooks) for agents (MCP motivating case)
records.text: ### Feature Description We need a deterministic “communication layer” between LlamaIndex agents and tool execution. **Core need** 1) Deterministic input preprocessing **before** tool execution - Example: an MCP billing tool expects an `id` field, but `id` must be filled/overridden deterministically (e.g., derived from authenticated session/customer context) — NOT chosen or hallucinated by the LLM. 2) Deterministic output postprocessing **after** tool returns and **before** the agent sees it - Example: tool returns ~300 fields; we need deterministic filtering down to 3 fields to avoid context bloat and keep agent behavior stable. **Observed limitation** With current agent+tools patterns, once tools are registered the agent generates tool-call JSON/args and invokes tools without an obvious *native* “intercept/transform” layer for: - tool-call input args (pre) - tool output (post) in a way that is reusable across tools (cross-cutting concern), and especially clean for MCP tools. **Proposed feature (medium-detail, not a full spec)** Support one (or a combination) of: - Agent/tool execution hook or middleware to transform tool inputs/outputs deterministically (pre/post). - First-class tool wrapper/adapter API pattern documented and supported for IO transforms (so it’s ergonomic + consistent). - Maintainer guidance on preferred placement: agent runner vs tool runner vs callback/event layer. **Minimal code example (current workaround vs desired)** _Current workaround (per-tool wrapper; works but doesn’t scale well across many tools and doesn’t feel “first-class”):_ ```python from llama_index.core.agent.workflow import FunctionAgent from llama_index.core.tools import FunctionTool # Deterministic value from outside the LLM (e.g., auth/session layer) SESSION_CUSTOMER_ID = "cust_123456" def call_mcp_billing(payload: dict) -> dict: """Placeholder: call MCP tool server and return raw JSON (~300 fields).""" # ... network call ... return {"balance": 12.34, "due_date": "2025-12-31", "status": "OPEN", "lots_more": "..."} # etc. def billing_lookup(question: str, id: str | None = None) -> dict: # PRE: deterministically override/ignore LLM-provided `id` payload = {"id": SESSION_CUSTOMER_ID, "question": question} raw = call_mcp_billing(payload) # POST: deterministically shrink tool output before it hits agent context return {k: raw.get(k) for k in ("balance", "due_date", "status")} billing_tool = FunctionTool.from_defaults( fn=billing_lookup, name="billing_lookup", description="Get billing info for the authenticated customer." ) agent = FunctionAgent(tools=[billing_tool]) # await agent.run("Why is my bill higher this month?") ```` *Desired ergonomics (illustrative API; not current):* ```python agent = FunctionAgent( tools=mcp_tools, tool_io_middleware=[ ToolIOMiddleware( before=lambda tool_name, args: override_id(args, SESSION_CUSTOMER_ID), after=lambda tool_name, out: filter_fields(out, tool_name), ) ], ) ``` **Notes** * LlamaIndex already supports `FunctionTool` callbacks that can override tool output content, but this does not address a general, reusable pre/post IO transform layer across arbitrary tools/tool specs (especially MCP). Docs/examples: * FunctionTool reference: [https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/framework-api-reference/tools/function/](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/framework-api-reference/tools/function/) * FunctionTool callback example: [https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/examples/tools/function_tool_callback/](https://developers.llamaindex.ai/python/examples/tools/function_tool_callback/) ### Reason We need deterministic tool I/O transforms for reliability and predictable integrations in production agent systems (MCP is a motivating case, but this is broadly useful for any tool calling). **Why this matters** - **Reliability & correctness:** LLM-chosen identifiers/fields can be wrong or inconsistent. Deterministically overriding fields like `id` prevents “random” tool calls and removes a class of failures. - **Compliance/auditability:** For regulated environments, having a deterministic tool-call envelope (and a deterministic “view” of tool outputs that the agent consumes) improves auditability and reduces risk. - **Cost/latency + quality:** Tool outputs with hundreds of fields create context bloat, increasing token usage and failure modes. Deterministic filtering (e.g., 300 → 3 fields) is a cross-cutting concern. - **Separation of concerns:** Forcing every tool to implement its own filtering/override logic duplicates effort and makes behavior inconsistent. **Workarounds being explored (with tradeoffs)** - Put pre/post logic inside the MCP tool itself (e.g., add `fields_to_return`) — shifts responsibility into every tool and doesn’t solve cross-cutting concerns. - Use agent only as a tool selector; execute tool calls deterministically outside the agent — reduces the value of integrated agent/tool patterns. **Related issues searched (not exact duplicates, but adjacent)** - Tool output / observability / callback-related discussions: https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/9770 - MCP + agents usage questions: https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19023 - Capturing raw tool outputs from workflows (adjacent to “postprocessing” needs): https://github.com/run-llama/llama_index/issues/19722 Keywords searched: “tool pre-processing”, “tool post-processing”, “tool middleware”, “agent tool hooks”, “callbacks tool input”, “tool output filtering”, “MCP”, “deterministic tool call”. ### Value of Feature **What this unlocks** - A consistent, maintainable way to enforce deterministic tool-call envelopes (e.g., override/fill `id` from trusted context) without relying on the LLM. - Deterministic, tool-specific (or global) output shaping to reduce context bloat and improve stability (e.g., 300 fields → 3 fields). - Cleaner MCP tool integrations where the agent remains responsible for “what to do next”, but the *communication layer* stays deterministic and policy-compliant. *

records.title: Integration proposal: memory store with verified transfer — export/import sealed memory bundles
records.text: I maintain [cognicore-env](https://github.com/cognicore-dev/cognicore-env) (open-source, MIT) — a memory layer for agents that speaks MCP and needs no vector database or embedding server (TF-IDF retrieval over pure stdlib). LlamaIndex has a memory abstraction and a broad store ecosystem; what no store provides is portability with provenance. Memory written in one LlamaIndex deployment stays there, and when teams do move it, it travels as text — no verification state, no history, no expiry. Proposal: a LlamaIndex memory integration where memories can be exported and imported as sealed bundles. Per memory: proof (command, result, exit code, output hash), chain of custody across agents, observed-until-reverified import semantics, trust decay across unverified hops, validity intervals (a fact verified in March is not evidence about April), and owner-per-concept for conflicts — the last two validated in a public design review with multi-team operators. Use case: a LlamaIndex agent that spent a month indexing and querying a codebase exports its verified conventions; another deployment (or a non-LlamaIndex agent) imports them and starts from evidence instead of zero. Happy to contribute the store integration plus a notebook example. The transfer machinery is implemented and tested across four platforms. Is this a fit for the integrations catalog?

records.title: [Feature Request]: Memory poisoning defense (OWASP ASI06) integration for agent memory stores
records.text: ### Feature Description OWASP recently published the **Top 10 for Agentic Applications**, which includes **ASI06: Memory Poisoning** — a threat specific to AI agents that persist memory across sessions. LlamaIndex's agent memory stores (ChatMemoryBuffer, VectorMemory, SimpleComposableMemory) are a prime target for this attack. A malicious user can craft inputs that get stored as "trusted" memories, which then influence future agent behavior — leaking data, taking unauthorized actions, or hijacking tool calls across sessions. The OWASP reference implementation for ASI06 is [agent-memory-guard](https://github.com/OWASP/www-project-agent-memory-guard) (Apache-2.0, pure Python, zero external dependencies): pip install agent-memory-guard Proposed integration: A GuardedMemory wrapper that implements LlamaIndex's BaseMemory interface, screening all put() and get() calls through the OWASP defense pipeline (prompt injection detection, integrity verification, policy enforcement). ### Reason LlamaIndex currently has no built-in defense for memory poisoning attacks. As agent use cases grow (especially multi-session, multi-user deployments), this becomes a critical security gap. The OWASP ASI06 reference implementation provides a drop-in solution. ### Value of Feature Provides OWASP-compliant memory security for LlamaIndex agents. Addresses a formally recognized threat category (ASI06) with a production-ready, zero-dependency implementation. Enables enterprise adoption of LlamaIndex agents where security compliance is required.

records.title: [Feature Request]: Trust scoring and interaction history for tool and agent reliability
records.text: ### Feature Description LlamaIndex agents can call tools, query external data sources, and delegate to sub-agents. But there's no way to track whether a particular tool or agent has been reliable across sessions. If your RAG pipeline queries an external API that returned bad data last time, or delegates to a sub-agent that failed 3 out of 5 recent tasks, nothing in LlamaIndex remembers that. I built a sidecar that records interactions between agents and tools bilaterally. Both the caller and the callee cosign a record of what happened. From the graph of those records you get trust scores, skill-specific reliability (this tool is good at code search but bad at summarization), Sybil detection, and full audit trails. New tools/agents start UNPROVEN and graduate through 5 trust tiers as their track record grows. Works as a transparent HTTP proxy (zero code changes) or through a Python SDK: ```python from trustchain import TrustClient tc = TrustClient() # before calling a tool: check its track record trust = tc.check_trust(tool_pubkey) if trust.tier < "ESTABLISHED" or trust.skill_reliability("retrieval") < 0.7: # use a different retriever or add verification ... # after the call: record what happened tc.record_interaction(counterparty=tool_pubkey, action="retrieval", quality=0.9) ``` Also has 7 MCP tools so MCP-capable agents can query trust natively. Verification works fully offline with just Ed25519 public keys. The interaction graph is a substrate you can build on. Trust scoring is just the first use. The same graph powers agent discovery (rank by reputation within a capability), behavioral anomaly detection, dispute resolution, and compliance audit trails. ### Reason LlamaIndex currently has no mechanism for cross-session tool/agent reliability tracking. If a tool returns bad results, the agent has no memory of that in the next session. Guardrails validate output format but not source reliability over time. ### Value of Feature - Agents make better delegation decisions based on actual track record, not just tool descriptions - Bad tools/agents get deprioritized automatically without manual curation - RAG pipelines become more reliable by routing to sources with proven retrieval quality - Full audit trail for compliance (EU AI Act Article 12 ready) Working implementation with a LlamaIndex adapter: https://github.com/viftode4/trustchain Live demo with 21 LLM agents in a trust-scored economy: http://5.161.255.238:8888

records.title: Proposal: Agent Threat Rules detection integration for LlamaIndex
records.text: I would like to propose an integration that exposes ATR-style threat detection as an instrumentation EventHandler in LlamaIndex, and I want to check the right shape before opening a PR given that CONTRIBUTING.md says new integration packages with their own pyproject.toml are auto-closed. What ATR is. The Agent Threat Rules standard at https://github.com/Agent-Threat-Rule/agent-threat-rules is an MIT-licensed detection catalog for LLM agents. The catalog targets prompt injection, system prompt extraction, indirect injection markers, credential exfiltration, shell command injection, SSRF cloud metadata, and similar attacker patterns specific to tool-using agents. Where it would fit in LlamaIndex. The cleanest integration point looks like the V2 instrumentation pipeline (llama_index.core.instrumentation, BaseEventHandler). A handler subscribed to AgentRunStepEvent, ToolCallStartEvent, ToolCallEndEvent, and CallStartEvent could match incoming text against the rule set and emit a new ThreatDetectionEvent into the same pipeline, which downstream observability tools like Phoenix, Langfuse, or OpenInference would already capture. The literalai callback at llama-index-integrations/callbacks/llama-index-callbacks-literalai is roughly the shape I am modeling against, including the get_dispatcher and add_event_handler pattern. Three options I can see, ordered from least to most invasive. Option 1 docs only: a worked example in docs/examples/observability that wires a small inline EventHandler subclass with a handful of regex rules and shows the detection signal flowing through the dispatcher. Useful but not a reusable building block. Option 2 small core helper: a thin generic ThreatDetectionEventHandler class in llama-index-core under callbacks or instrumentation that takes a list of rule tuples and a strategy ('block' raises, 'flag' emits an event), with no opinionated rule defaults. Users would supply their own rules or load the ATR catalog with a few lines of code. Option 3 separately published integration: a PyPI package outside this repo, since CONTRIBUTING.md is clear that new integration packages with new pyproject.toml are auto-closed. I am happy to do this; I would just want to know if a docs example or core helper is welcome alongside it so users discover it. Question for maintainers: which of these three would you accept a PR for, and does the answer change if no new dependency is added (the implementation needs only stdlib re plus the existing instrumentation API)? MIT license either way. Edit (2026-10-15): corrected the license (ATR is MIT, not Apache-2.0, as noted in my first reply below), dropped a category count, and removed a sentence citing other projects' use of ATR, which shouldn't have been offered as support for this proposal.

records.title: [Feature Request]: Support Multiple Embeddings per Node
records.text: ### Feature Description Store multiple embeddings for the same BaseNode and all of its derivatives (TextNode, Document, ImageNode, etc.). Currently BaseNode has a field `embedding` which is type-enforced as `Optional[List[float]]` by Pydantic. This restricts each node to having only a single embedding. I would like to store multiple embeddings for the same node (e.g. dense embedding, sparse embedding, etc.). These embeddings may have different dimensionality or format (e.g. sparse embeddings are often represented as a key-value mapping instead of array). This could be implemented by allowing the `embedding` field on BaseNode to be compatible with a dictionary of embeddings in addition to the current single-embedding implementation (e.g. `Optional[List[float] | Dict[str, Any]]`). The proposal is to accomplish something similar to the API provided by Qdrant Vectorstore where multiple embedding vectors can be associated with a single payload (analogous to llama_index node). Reference from Qdrant: - https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/collections/#collection-with-multiple-vectors - https://qdrant.tech/documentation/concepts/points/#update-vectors The alternative to modifying the base node classes would be to enable easy addition of custom node types into llama-index. Currently this is possible, but is not straightforward because many llama-index components (node parsers, splitters, ingestion cache, ingestion pipeline, etc.) all assume the default node types and validate node types using pydantic. Introduction of custom node types currently requires subclassing most of the llama-index components to support custom node types. ### Reason I am unsure if changing the field type for `BaseNode.embeddings` will have unintended effects across the rest of llama-index components. Many components may assume that the `embeddings` field contains a single embedding instead of a dictionary of multiple embeddings. ### Value of Feature Avoid requiring users to heavily customize llama-index in order to support multi-embedding applications (e.g. hybrid search). Currently the Qdrant vectorstore implementation implements a special work-around to enable hybrid mode by generating sparse embeddings within the Qdrant vectorstore implementation. This assumes 2 embedding models will be used (one for dense and one for sparse). With the new [BAAI/BGE-M3 embedding](https://huggingface.co/BAAI/bge-m3), multiple embeddings can be generated from a single model call, which would make the current Qdrant vectorstore hybrid implementation inefficient.

records.text: ### Bug Description Version Info: ``` llama-index 0.12.48 llama-index-core 0.12.48 llama-index-llms-bedrock-converse 0.7.4 ``` I've been trying to experiment with the [Memory class](https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/stable/module_guides/deploying/agents/memory/) as this is the latest recommendation in the documentation (per the deprecation of the other memory modules/classes). During my testing, I wanted to look at [Long-Term Memory](https://docs.llamaindex.ai/en/stable/module_guides/deploying/agents/memory/#long-term-memory) and was starting with the `FactExtractionMemoryBlock`. I opted to use BedrockConverse for my `FactExtractionMemoryBlock` LLM class, opting for Claude 3.5 Haiku as the model. From there, I then plugged the `Memory` instance into my agent workflow and began: ```python memory = Memory.from_defaults( session_id="foo-session", token_limit=40_000, chat_history_token_ratio=0.02, # trying to force short-term to long-term insert_method="user", memory_blocks=[ FactExtractionMemoryBlock( name="extracted_info", llm=BedrockConverse(model="us.anthropic.claude-3-5-haiku-20241022-v1:0"), max_facts=50, priority=1, ) ] ) agent = FunctionAgent( # NOTE: different model than FactExtractionMemoryBlock llm=BedrockConverse(model="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-20250514-v1:0") name="foo-agent", description="foo-description", system_prompt="...", # one or more tools tools=[FunctionTool.from_defaults(fn=tool_a, name="tool_a"), FunctionTool.from_defaults(fn=tool_b, name="tool_b")] ) # I know we can run FunctionAgent directly now, but this is what I had for the test workflow = AgentWorkflow( agents=[agent], root_agent=agent.name, ) handler = workflow.run(user_msg="...", memory=memory) async for event in handler.stream_events(): ... ``` After asking a question that would cause tool invocation, I eventually started seeing the following error **as the `FactExtractionMemoryBlock` began to kick in**: ``` [llama_index.llms.bedrock_converse.utils] [before_sleep:65] - Retrying llama_index.llms.bedrock_converse.utils.converse_with_retry_async. ._conversion_with_retry in 4.0 seconds as it raised ValidationException: An error occurred (ValidationException) when calling the Converse operation: The toolConfig field must be defined when using toolUse and toolResult content blocks.. ...repeats a few times, per retry logic... ``` taking just the error: ``` An error occurred (ValidationException) when calling the Converse operation: The toolConfig field must be defined when using toolUse and toolResult content blocks.. ``` which eventually caused the workflow to fail. I'm not sure if I'm doing something wrong with `Memory` and/or `FactExtractionMemoryBlock`, or if this is an issue within `BedrockConverse`. I can confirm though that this arises when `FactExtractionMemoryBlock` makes the LLM call to BedrockConverse (observed by seeing the payload sent to the converse operation). ### Version 0.12.48 ### Steps to Reproduce ```python memory = Memory.from_defaults( session_id="foo-session", token_limit=40_000, chat_history_token_ratio=0.02, # trying to force short-term to long-term insert_method="user", memory_blocks=[ FactExtractionMemoryBlock( name="extracted_info", llm=BedrockConverse(model="us.anthropic.claude-3-5-haiku-20241022-v1:0"), max_facts=50, priority=1, ) ] ) agent = FunctionAgent( # NOTE: different model than FactExtractionMemoryBlock llm=BedrockConverse(model="us.anthropic.claude-sonnet-4-20250514-v1:0") name="foo-agent", description="foo-description", system_prompt="...", # one or more tools tools=[FunctionTool.from_defaults(fn=tool_a, name="tool_a"), FunctionTool.from_defaults(fn=tool_b, name="tool_b")] ) # I know we can run FunctionAgent directly now, but this is what I had for the test workflow = AgentWorkflow( agents=[agent], root_agent=agent.name, ) handler = workflow.run(user_msg="...", memory=memory) async for event in handler.stream_events(): ... ``` ``` An error occurred (ValidationException) when calling the Converse operation: The toolConfig field must be defined when using toolUse and toolResult content blocks.. ```

records.title: [Bug]: CondensePlusContextChatEngine.astream_chat silently aborts generation and yields 'Empty Response' when Retriever returns 0 nodes
records.text: ### Bug Description When using `CondensePlusContextChatEngine` with an asynchronous stream (`astream_chat`), if the provided `Retriever` (e.g., `QueryFusionRetriever` or `VectorIndexRetriever`) returns `0` nodes (which can happen frequently with valid metadata filters like tenant IDs), the Chat Engine silently aborts the LLM generation process. Instead of passing the system prompt and the user query to the LLM with an empty context, the synthesizer (called via `_arun_c3` -> `asynthesize`) evaluates to an empty node list and completely skips the LLM API call. It instantly returns a hardcoded `"Empty Response"` string wrapped in an `AsyncStreamingResponse`. This is highly problematic for production RAG systems (like multi-tenant architectures), where a user might ask a general question or have an empty vector space on their first day. Instead of the LLM answering naturally leveraging its baseline knowledge and the System Prompt, the application receives a silent `"Empty Response"` in less than 1 second, with no exceptions raised, masking the behavior. [llamaindex_bug_report.md](https://github.com/user-attachments/files/25783280/llamaindex_bug_report.md) ### Version Python 3.12.x LlamaIndex v0.10.x LLM Provider: Agnostic (Tested with Ollama, but reproducible via OpenAI due to synthesizer logic) ### Steps to Reproduce import asyncio from llama_index.core import Document, VectorStoreIndex from llama_index.core.chat_engine import CondensePlusContextChatEngine from llama_index.llms.ollama import Ollama # or OpenAI async def main(): # 1. Create an empty index (or one where filters will yield 0 nodes) index = VectorStoreIndex.from_documents([]) retriever = index.as_retriever(similarity_top_k=2) # 2. Setup LLM llm = Ollama(model="qwen2.5:0.5b") # Ensure model is running locally # 3. Build CondensePlusContextChatEngine engine = CondensePlusContextChatEngine.from_defaults( retriever=retriever, llm=llm, system_prompt="You are a helpful AI." ) # 4. Attempt to trigger Async Stream print("Sending query...") chat_stream = await engine.astream_chat("Hello, can you help me?") full_text = "" async for token in chat_stream.async_response_gen(): full_text += token print(f"Final Response: '{full_text}'") # Expected output: "Hello! Yes, I can help you..." # Actual output: "Empty Response" (Instantly, no LLM call dispatched) if __name__ == "__main__": asyncio.run(main()) ### Relevant Logs/Tracbacks ```shell INFO:src.agent:📂 Initializing local search tool (RAG)... INFO:src.agent: ✓ RAG tool initialized successfully INFO:src.engine_builder:⚙️ Configuring Hybrid Search (Vector + BM25)... INFO:src.engine_builder: 🔍 Tenant Filter applied: Jeferson WARNING:src.engine_builder: ⚠️ No documents found in ChromaDB for BM25. INFO:src.engine_builder: 🧠 Engine initialized via OLLAMA with model qwen2.5:0.5b [STARTING ASTREAM_CHAT TRACE] INFO:llama_index.core.chat_engine.condense_plus_context:Condensed question: Hello Sovereign! This is a test being sent directly from N8N via Webhook in the Cybrid network. # Execution HALTS in less than 1.2s without dispatching any POST request to /api/chat ==== DEBUG RESPONSE ==== TYPE: FULL TEXT FINAL: 'Empty Response' chat_stream.response: 'Empty Response' ```

records.title: [Feature Request]: Memory (SQLAlchemy chat store) serves edited, replayed and re-owned messages as genuine context; aget() never signals a changed store
records.text: ### Feature Description Measured on llama-index-core 0.14.24, SQLite via aiosqlite, macOS arm64, Python 3.12, with the open MIT suite agmi (https://github.com/tech4biz-yasha/agmi, row `llamaindex-memory-sqlite`). Method: seed a session through `Memory.aput_messages()`, apply one edit directly to the `llama_index_memory` table with no keys, open a fresh `Memory` on the same database, read through `Memory.aget()`, and record what the library does. Result: all eight storage-level edits are accepted, meaning `aget()` returns without raising and the edited history becomes the agent's context. T1 text changed inside a message's `data` T2 newest messages deleted, so the agent resumes from an older state T3 one message removed from the middle T4 two messages swapped T5 a new message inserted by the attacker T6 another session's message copied over this session's row, `key` kept (user B's message served as user A's) T7 an older message of the same session copied over the newest T8 the row's `timestamp` rewritten, text untouched. Separately, rewriting `key` moves a message into another session's context, and setting `status` to archived silently drops it from context; neither raises. Reproduction and pinned tests: https://github.com/tech4biz-yasha/agmi/blob/main/tests/test_llamaindex_memory.py Explainer per edit: https://agentmemoryintegrity.org/edits.html I understand the store may assume a trusted database. Two things would help users whose memory database is shared, backed up or reachable by other services: a note in the Memory docs that rows carry no integrity protection, and optionally a keyed MAC per row over `key + position + status + data`, checked in `aget()`. The reference store in agmi (`agmi/adapters/reference_atrest.py`) shows the minimum that rejects all eight. Happy to open a PR for either, and I will re-measure and update the public row when anything changes. ### Reason Anyone who can write to the memory database (a shared database, a backup restore, another service) can change, delete, reorder, forge or move messages between sessions, and the agent treats the result as its own history. Today there is nothing in the docs that says the store carries no integrity protection, so users assume it does. ### Value of Feature A docs note costs nothing and sets the right expectation. An optional keyed check on read would let users who need it reject an edited history instead of acting on it, without changing behaviour for anyone else. I can open the PR.

records.title: Ask HN: How to deal with shipping AI-written code you don't understand?
records.text: If you take a step back here, there has always been a group of people who have "shipped code to production" — in the sense of being responsible for the software that was produced -- without ever reading it or knowing it in detail. I am talking about your engineering management. Maybe not your line manager but certainly your director. I think a useful perspective is "How does engineering management control software quality?" You will know the answers to this question: testing practices, design documents, SLAs, release management. You will know this because you almost certainly have to comply with some of these as a SWE. All of those practices exist because code produced by humans is not perfectly reliable and thus there need to be checks and risk reduction steps to manage the software that is shipped. The way I view agents is that all of us have become engineering managers now. So those tools are now your tools. You set up the practices and frameworks and make the agents use them. If you set them up right you can be very confident in what the agents wrote without ever reading it. Now you're not going to go from nothing to "Hey I ship code I've never read" overnight. It takes work. You have to set up your project carefully so that the agents can’t make mistakes. But all you have to do is be systematic about it. Every time the agents do something stupid or they ship a bug, you think, "How do I put something in place to prevent this entire class of bugs from happening again?" As you iterate this process, you will continuously be ruling out entire classes of bugs and eventually you'll be able to trust the agents. Example: I had a bug, or a class of bugs, where agents would write a database migration and it would be wrong. It would get rolled out and the database would be broken. I fixed this by putting in a migration testing framework where there was data written in an old schema, then the migrations would run on that data. Then you could write tests on the expected result at any point after any migrations. Then, I put in place a rule: if you write a database migration you have to write a migration test. That fixed the problem. I have never had a migration failure since. So this is not some magical process. It's going to take you hard work to set up your system with all of this infrastructure to make the agents maximally productive. But as you iteratively improve your system, you can reach a place where you can have agents ship code without reading it. It's not just about making the system work but it's also about building your trust in the system that you have. I routinely ship code without reading it now and I think I've shipped about two bugs in the past two months (and I’ve written ~500k LOC in that time). And one of those bugs was very explicitly my fault for telling the agents they could violate one of the frameworks in place (oops).

records.title: Migrations turn code itself into state
records.text: Unlike most languages, which tell the computer how to do a task step by step, SQL says what you want, and the database decides how . That makes databases vastly easier to use, yet SQL can be harder to build with than the rest of the app, even code that spells out every step. The problem is that software always changes. Usually that means changing, adding, or deleting code. But changing how a database organizes its data requires "migrations" -- directions from its current state to its desired state. Because migrations are an inextricable part of life with SQL databases, (much of) SQL code in practice runs in the order it's written, so to understand any bit of SQL you must understand every bit that ran before it... and new code gets harder to write as the code base grows. Consider two programs controlling a robot: Brittle: 1. drive 100 meters forward 2. turn 90 degrees right 3. drive another 50 meters Resilient: 1. turn right at the stop light 2. stop at the first house The brittle version is longer (i.e. worse), but the key issue is that, like SQL in practice, each step only makes sense if you know all the steps before it. Take "turn 90 degrees right". It takes you through the stop light or off a cliff, depending on where the prior commands landed you. Not so with "turn right at the stop light". Run it at the wrong time and you may turn at the wrong light, but you won't turn into a car, a house, a wall, or off a cliff because you weren't where you thought. It's much easier to reason about, build, and maintain. This is why good engineers squeeze state handling into the smallest volume of code possible, and why the whole family of functional languages exists. But with SQL, the code isn't just handling state; the code itself is state. There's a reasonable reason: the database, unless empty, is state, so changes must consider what's in it. It's so painful that two approaches emerged largely to sidestep it. ORMs The 90s saw TOPLink and later Enterprise JavaBeans: Object Relational Mappers (ORMs), which mapped non-SQL code to SQL. They let engineers write ordinary code in modules, files, and functions. It was like ordering in a foreign country from a waiter who speaks both languages but is native in neither: you usually get what you asked for, but not always. Some were better than others, but every real system leaned on the escape hatch they all have: raw SQL -- speaking to the chef directly in the local language. Then SQL was sprinkled through another language's source, hard to reason about again, and the chef got contradictory orders from you and the waiter. ORMs also brought migration tools (Rails migrations, Alembic) that made the tower of changes easier to write but no easier to read. NoSQL Then came a global revolt against SQL, somewhere between Google's Bigtable paper in 2006 and 2009, when Cassandra, MongoDB, CouchDB, Redis, and others proudly joined the NoSQL movement. Mongo was easy to start and iterate on, but SQL still won for many reasons. Chief among them: the data model didn't magically disappear -- it became an emergent property of the code, spreading the same poison migrations carried into the entire code base. The code became state. So after a long hype cycle, Postgres became the most-used database in the 2023 Stack Overflow developer survey, and SQL reasserted its dominance. The end state There are a variety of schema differs out there -- including a variety aimed just at Postgres. We couldn't find one that was both open source and worked on our code so we wrote pgdeclare. It lets people write in SQL but describe the final state without building up an ever less stable tower of changes. Reverse jenga still ends up with a pile of blocks on the floor -- it's just a bigger mess. To set expectations: some change management is inevitable and we provide our own escape hatch for that. Hopefully it works for you, and if not, pull requests are very welcome.

records.title: Personal software factories are a waste of time
records.text: I mean, my personal software factory was building one small project with an overtly enthusiastic and strict set of precommit checks that all must pass. Then starting every new project with "using the same precommit checks from project X" Using Elixir, Phoenix, LiveView and Ash for everything creates a very well defined and verifiable structure for every part of the codebase with a precommit that looks like this: precommit: [ "compile --warnings-as-errors", # Fail compilation if any warnings exist "deps.unlock --check-unused", # Fail if unused dependencies are unlocked "deps.audit", # Scan dependencies for known security vulnerabilities "cmd mix hex.audit", # Audit Hex packages for retired or vulnerable versions "migrations.safety", # Check database migrations for unsafe operations "format --check-formatted", # Verify code matches the formatter style "credo --strict", # Run strict static code analysis checks "sobelow --exit --threshold high --skip", # Fail on high-confidence security issues only "ash.codegen --check", # Ensure Ash generated code is up to date "usage_rules.sync --check", # Verify usage rules are synchronized "cmd bun run lint", # If there's JS beyond LiveView "test" # Run the full test suite ] The result has been excellent consistency across my code base and the AI learns fast how it should be working. Everything comes out very readable if I want to dig into something. For the most part, everything I ask for gets 1 shotted with this approach with typically rare minor tweaks and refinements.

records.title: Pg_vectorsearch: An index that is faster than pgvector's IVFFlat and HNSW
records.text: A couple preliminary findings if you are considering adopting this extension to replace your previous pgvector's HNSW indexing. - pg_vectorsearch uses a quantized IVF index called PRISM. PRISM caps at 1968 dimensions for vectors. If your previous HNSW index has more dimensions than that, you're SOL (at least for now until they fix that). - pg_vectorsearch requires Postgres version 18 or above. If you run PG versions below that you need to migrate your database first. Many legacy PG production environment are way dated on PG 14 or 15, migration is prohibitively high cost to just try this out. - pg_vectorsearch shipped yesterday and it's obviously alpha. Hasn't been battle tested in production environments outside of Timescale's. Also since it's so new, it isn't on Azure's allowed-extension list or any other Hyperscale's managed PG instances' allowed extension list. It takes time to graduate from alpha and mature. So if you run managaed PG instances from hyperscaler's cloud, you're SOL (at least for now until this matures into those ecosystems) or you have to migrate to a PG 18 self-hosted.
